note: Pope Adrian V's wish to get back to his penance, which ended their talk in Canto 19. Dante wanted to ask more.
His curiosity, pictured as a sponge lifted from the water before it has soaked up all it could hold.

quote: like walkers on a wall beside the battlements
note: The souls of the greedy lie so thick along the outer edge of the terrace that the poets must keep close to the cliff, like sentries on the narrow walk behind a castle's parapet.

quote: the sickness that infects the entire world
note: Avarice, the greedy love of wealth. For Dante it is the root of the disorder of his time, in the Church, in Florence and among kings.

context: The beast that drove Dante back from the hill in Inferno 1, here named outright as greed.

note: The belief that the turning of the stars brings about changes on earth, discussed in Canto 16. Dante looks to the heavens for a sign of the rescuer.

context: In Inferno 1, Virgil foretold a hound that would hunt the she-wolf back to Hell. Dante asks when.
The first of three examples of poverty and generosity freely chosen, the opposite of greed. Mary gave birth to Christ in a stable.

note: The stable at Bethlehem. Mary laid the child in a manger "because there was no room for them in the inn" (Luke 2:7).
Gaius Fabricius, a Roman consul of the 3rd century BC, famous for his honesty. He refused the rich gifts offered by Rome's enemies, among them King Pyrrhus, and died poor.

Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra in Asia Minor in the 4th century. In his legend a poor man was about to sell his three daughters into prostitution. Nicholas threw three bags of gold through their window at night, so that each could marry. He is the origin of Santa Claus.
Dante offers what the living can give the dead in Purgatory: prayers, his own or those he can ask of others, which shorten a soul's time of penance.
The Capetian dynasty, the royal house of France. In 1300 its branches ruled France, Naples and Provence, and in Dante's view they darkened all of Europe.

quote: Douai and Ghent and Lille and Bruges
note: The chief towns of Flanders, which King Philip the Fair of France seized by force and bad faith from 1297. The vengeance came in 1302, when Flemish townsmen destroyed a French army of knights at Courtrai. Dante, writing later, has Hugh pray for what had already happened.

context: Dante blends him with his father, Hugh the Great, the real power in France a generation earlier. He lies among the greedy and condemns his own descendants for their greed.

note: From 1060 to Dante's day, every king of France was named Philip or Louis.

quote: the son of a Parisian butcher
note: A legend current in Dante's time, and false. Hugh Capet's father was Hugh the Great, duke of the Franks. Dante uses the story to give the proud French kings a low origin.
The Carolingians, the line of Charlemagne, which ended in 987.

A monk. The last Carolingian claimant, Charles of Lorraine, died in prison, not in a monastery. Dante seems to have confused him with the last king of the earlier dynasty, the Merovingians, who was deposed in 751 and put in a monastery.
Hugh Capet's son was Robert II, crowned alongside him. If the speaker is thought of as Hugh the Great, the son is Hugh Capet himself. Dante's history of these kings is muddled.
The vacant throne, a crown that has lost its king.
The kings of France were anointed with holy oil at their coronation.

In 1246 Charles of Anjou, brother of the king of France, married Beatrice, heiress of the count of Provence, and the rich county passed to the French royal house. Hugh dates his family's shamelessness from that gain.
Savage sarcasm, repeated three times as a rhyme word in the Italian. Each crime is "made up for" by a worse one.
Lands held by the kings of England as vassals of France. Normandy was taken from King John in 1204. Gascony, and Ponthieu with it, were seized from Edward I by Philip the Fair in the 1290s.

context: He came to Italy in 1265 at the pope's invitation. Hugh counts two killings against him.

note: The last heir of the imperial house of Hohenstaufen, grandson of Frederick II. At sixteen he came to Italy to win back his family's kingdom. Charles defeated him at Tagliacozzo in 1268 and had him beheaded in the marketplace of Naples.

context: He died in 1274 on his way to a Church council. A rumor, repeated here, said that Charles had him poisoned. Historians give it no credit.
The journey is set in 1300, so Hugh foretells as future what Dante, writing later, already knew. This is the event that cost Dante his home.

note: The lance of Judas is treachery. Charles came to Florence without an army, as a peacemaker, and betrayed the city he had sworn to pacify.

context: In November 1301 Charles of Valois let the exiled Black Guelphs back into the city. They looted and burned their rivals' houses for days, and in the purge that followed Dante was banished.

note: A jab at his nickname, Charles Lackland. He never won a kingdom of his own, and his campaign in Sicily in 1302 ended in failure.

context: The Italian says he "once came out of a ship as a prisoner": he was captured in a sea battle off Naples in 1284 by the admiral of Aragon. That is how Dante identifies him.

note: In 1305 Charles II married his young daughter Beatrice to Azzo VIII d'Este, the much older lord of Ferrara, reportedly in exchange for a large sum.
The lily, emblem of the kings of France.

Anagni, a hill town southeast of Rome, the birthplace of Pope Boniface VIII and his summer residence. In September 1303 agents of the French king stormed the papal palace there and took the pope prisoner.

quote: Christ made captive in his own vicar
context: Dante hated Boniface and places him in Hell. But the pope is Christ's vicar, his deputy on earth, and Dante sees the assault on him as a second Passion of Christ. The townspeople freed Boniface after a few days, and he died within weeks.

note: The bitter drink offered to Christ on the cross (Matthew 27:34).
Christ died between two thieves who died with him. The pope's captors, the French minister Guillaume de Nogaret and the Roman noble Sciarra Colonna, lived on unpunished.

context: Pilate handed Christ over to his enemies. Philip handed Christ's vicar over to the Colonna family, Boniface's sworn enemies.

note: The Knights Templar, a rich military order of monks. In 1307 Philip had its members in France arrested on charges of heresy and took its wealth. "Without decree" means without the lawful authority of the Church. The sails are those of a pirate.
God's punishment of the French house, already fixed in his counsel but not yet seen on earth. Knowing that it is coming makes his anger calm.
Mary, who conceived Christ by the Holy Spirit. Hugh now answers Dante's second question, about the praises he was calling out.
By day the souls call out examples of generosity and willing poverty. By night they call out seven examples of greed punished, taken in turn from myth, the Bible and history.

Not the sculptor of the myth but the king of Tyre in the Aeneid, brother of Dido. He secretly murdered Dido's husband Sychaeus, his own kinsman, for his treasure. Dido fled with the gold and founded Carthage.

The king of Phrygia who asked the god Bacchus that everything he touched turn to gold. His food and drink turned to gold too, and he had to beg to have the gift taken back. Ovid tells the story in the Metamorphoses.

After the fall of Jericho, all its treasure was to be given to God. The Israelite Achan secretly kept some gold, silver and a fine cloak. When the theft was found out, Joshua had him stoned to death (Joshua 7).
Ananias and Sapphira, early Christians in Jerusalem. They sold a piece of land, kept back part of the price and lied about it to the apostle Peter. Each fell dead at his feet (Acts 5).
The minister of a Syrian king, sent to seize the treasure of the Temple in Jerusalem. A horse with a fearsome rider in golden armor appeared and struck him down with its hooves (2 Maccabees 3).

During the Trojan War, King Priam sent his youngest son, Polydorus, with a store of gold to Polymnestor, king of Thrace, for safekeeping. When Troy fell, Polymnestor killed the boy and kept the gold. Virgil and Ovid both tell the story.

Marcus Licinius Crassus, the richest man in Rome and the political partner of Caesar and Pompey. He was killed in 53 BC on a campaign against the Parthians. The story went that their king had molten gold poured into the dead man's mouth, mocking his thirst for it.
The cause is explained in Canto 21. The mountain shakes, and every soul on it gives praise, whenever one soul finishes its penance and is free to rise to Heaven.
An island in the Aegean Sea. In myth it drifted loose on the waves, shaken by the sea, until the goddess Latona took refuge there and it was fixed in place.
Leto in Greek. Pregnant by Jupiter and hunted across the world by his jealous wife Juno, she gave birth on Delos to the twins Apollo and Diana, the gods of the sun and the moon: heaven's two eyes.
In Dante's text the souls sing it in Latin, Gloria in excelsis Deo. It is the song of the angels on the night of Christ's birth (Luke 2:14). A soul's release into Heaven is greeted like the Nativity.
The shepherds near Bethlehem, to whom the angels announced the birth of Christ. The poets stand as amazed as they were.
